name: Component Firmware
desc: Adversaries may modify component firmware to persist on systems. Some adversaries may employ sophisticated means to compromise computer components and install malicious firmware that will execute adversary code outside of the operating syst

name: Bootkit
desc: Adversaries may use bootkits to persist on systems. A bootkit is a malware variant that modifies the boot sectors of a hard drive, allowing malicious code to execute before a computer's operating system has loaded.

name: ROMMONkit
desc: Adversaries may abuse the ROM Monitor (ROMMON) by loading an unauthorized firmware with adversary code to provide persistent access and manipulate device behavior that is difficult to detect.

name: TFTP Boot
desc: Adversaries may abuse netbooting to load an unauthorized network device operating system from a Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) server.

name: Create or Modify System Process
desc: Adversaries may create or modify system-level processes to repeatedly execute malicious payloads as part of persistence. When operating systems boot up, they can start processes that perform background system functions.

name: Launch Agent
desc: Adversaries may create or modify launch agents to repeatedly execute malicious payloads as part of persistence.

name: Systemd Service
desc: Adversaries may create or modify systemd services to repeatedly execute malicious payloads as part of persistence.

name: Windows Service
desc: Adversaries may create or modify Windows services to repeatedly execute malicious payloads as part of persistence. When Windows boots up, it starts programs or applications called services that perform background system functions.

name: Launch Daemon
desc: Adversaries may create or modify Launch Daemons to execute malicious payloads as part of persistence. Launch Daemons are plist files used to interact with Launchd, the service management framework used by macOS.

name: Container Service
desc: Adversaries may create or modify container or container cluster management tools that run as daemons, agents, or services on individual hosts.

name: Event Triggered Execution
desc: Adversaries may establish persistence and/or elevate privileges using system mechanisms that trigger execution based on specific events.

name: Change Default File Association
desc: Adversaries may establish persistence by executing malicious content triggered by a file type association. When a file is opened, the default program used to open the file (also called the file association or handler) is checked.

name: Screensaver
desc: Adversaries may establish persistence by executing malicious content triggered by user inactivity.

name: Windows Management Instrumentation Event Subscription
desc: Adversaries may establish persistence and elevate privileges by executing malicious content triggered by a Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) event subscription.

name: Unix Shell Configuration Modification
desc: Adversaries may establish persistence through executing malicious commands triggered by a user’s shell. User Unix Shells execute several configuration scripts at different points throughout the session based on events.

name: Trap
desc: Adversaries may establish persistence by executing malicious content triggered by an interrupt signal. The trap command allows programs and shells to specify commands that will be executed upon receiving interrupt signals.

name: LC_LOAD_DYLIB Addition
desc: Adversaries may establish persistence by executing malicious content triggered by the execution of tainted binaries. Mach-O binaries have a series of headers that are used to perform certain operations when a binary is loaded.

name: Netsh Helper DLL
desc: Adversaries may establish persistence by executing malicious content triggered by Netsh Helper DLLs. Netsh.exe (also referred to as Netshell) is a command-line scripting utility used to interact with the network configuration of a system.

name: Accessibility Features
desc: Adversaries may establish persistence and/or elevate privileges by executing malicious content triggered by accessibility features.

name: AppCert DLLs
desc: Adversaries may establish persistence and/or elevate privileges by executing malicious content triggered by AppCert DLLs loaded into processes.

name: AppInit DLLs
desc: Adversaries may establish persistence and/or elevate privileges by executing malicious content triggered by AppInit DLLs loaded into processes.

name: Application Shimming
desc: Adversaries may establish persistence and/or elevate privileges by executing malicious content triggered by application shims.

name: Image File Execution Options Injection
desc: Adversaries may establish persistence and/or elevate privileges by executing malicious content triggered by Image File Execution Options (IFEO) debuggers. IFEOs enable a developer to attach a debugger to an application.

name: PowerShell Profile
desc: Adversaries may gain persistence and elevate privileges by executing malicious content triggered by PowerShell profiles.

name: Emond
desc: Adversaries may gain persistence and elevate privileges by executing malicious content triggered by the Event Monitor Daemon (emond).

name: Component Object Model Hijacking
desc: Adversaries may establish persistence by executing malicious content triggered by hijacked references to Component Object Model (COM) objects.

name: Installer Packages
desc: Adversaries may establish persistence and elevate privileges by using an installer to trigger the execution of malicious content.

name: Udev Rules
desc: Adversaries may maintain persistence through executing malicious content triggered using udev rules.

name: Python Startup Hooks
desc: Adversaries may achieve persistence by leveraging Python’s startup mechanisms, including path configuration (`.pth`) files and the `sitecustomize.py` or `usercustomize.py` modules.

name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution
desc: Adversaries may configure system settings to automatically execute a program during system boot or logon to maintain persistence or gain higher-level privileges on compromised systems.

name: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
desc: Adversaries may achieve persistence by adding a program to a startup folder or referencing it with a Registry run key.

name: Authentication Package
desc: Adversaries may abuse authentication packages to execute DLLs when the system boots. Windows authentication package DLLs are loaded by the Local Security Authority (LSA) process at system start.

name: Time Providers
desc: Adversaries may abuse time providers to execute DLLs when the system boots. The Windows Time service (W32Time) enables time synchronization across and within domains.

name: Winlogon Helper DLL
desc: Adversaries may abuse features of Winlogon to execute DLLs and/or executables when a user logs in.

name: Security Support Provider
desc: Adversaries may abuse security support providers (SSPs) to execute DLLs when the system boots. Windows SSP DLLs are loaded into the Local Security Authority (LSA) process at system start.

name: Kernel Modules and Extensions
desc: Adversaries may modify the kernel to automatically execute programs on system boot. Loadable Kernel Modules (LKMs) are pieces of code that can be loaded and unloaded into the kernel upon demand.

name: Re-opened Applications
desc: Adversaries may modify plist files to automatically run an application when a user logs in.

name: LSASS Driver
desc: Adversaries may modify or add LSASS drivers to obtain persistence on compromised systems. The Windows security subsystem is a set of components that manage and enforce the security policy for a computer or domain.

name: Shortcut Modification
desc: Adversaries may create or modify shortcuts that can execute a program during system boot or user login.

name: Port Monitors
desc: Adversaries may use port monitors to run an adversary supplied DLL during system boot for persistence or privilege escalation. A port monitor can be set through the AddMonitor API call to set a DLL to be loaded at startup.

name: Print Processors
desc: Adversaries may abuse print processors to run malicious DLLs during system boot for persistence and/or privilege escalation. Print processors are DLLs that are loaded by the print spooler service, `spoolsv.exe`, during boot.

name: XDG Autostart Entries
desc: Adversaries may add or modify XDG Autostart Entries to execute malicious programs or commands when a user’s desktop environment is loaded at login. XDG Autostart entries are available for any XDG-compliant Linux system.

name: Active Setup
desc: Adversaries may achieve persistence by adding a Registry key to the Active Setup of the local machine. Active Setup is a Windows mechanism that is used to execute programs when a user logs in.

name: Login Items
desc: Adversaries may add login items to execute upon user login to gain persistence or escalate privileges. Login items are applications, documents, folders, or server connections that are automatically launched when a user logs in.

name: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism
desc: Adversaries may circumvent mechanisms designed to control privilege elevation to gain higher-level permissions.

name: Setuid and Setgid
desc: An adversary may abuse configurations where an application has the setuid or setgid bits set in order to get code running in a different (and possibly more privileged) user’s context.

name: Bypass User Account Control
desc: Adversaries may bypass UAC mechanisms to elevate process privileges on system. Windows User Account Control (UAC) allows a program to elevate its privileges (tracked as integrity levels ranging from low to high) to perform a task under admi

name: Sudo and Sudo Caching
desc: Adversaries may perform sudo caching and/or use the sudoers file to elevate privileges. Adversaries may do this to execute commands as other users or spawn processes with higher privileges.

name: Elevated Execution with Prompt
desc: Adversaries may leverage the AuthorizationExecuteWithPrivileges API to escalate privileges by prompting the user for credentials.

name: Temporary Elevated Cloud Access
desc: Adversaries may abuse permission configurations that allow them to gain temporarily elevated access to cloud resources.

name: TCC Manipulation
desc: Adversaries can manipulate or abuse the Transparency, Consent, & Control (TCC) service or database to grant malicious executables elevated permissions.

name: Use Alternate Authentication Material
desc: Adversaries may use alternate authentication material, such as password hashes, Kerberos tickets, and application access tokens, in order to move laterally within an environment and bypass normal system access controls.

name: Application Access Token
desc: Adversaries may use stolen application access tokens to bypass the typical authentication process and access restricted accounts, information, or services on remote systems.

name: Pass the Hash
desc: Adversaries may “pass the hash” using stolen password hashes to move laterally within an environment, bypassing normal system access controls.

name: Pass the Ticket
desc: Adversaries may “pass the ticket” using stolen Kerberos tickets to move laterally within an environment, bypassing normal system access controls.

name: Web Session Cookie
desc: Adversaries can use stolen session cookies to authenticate to web applications and services. This technique bypasses some multi-factor authentication protocols since the session is already authenticated.

name: Unsecured Credentials
desc: Adversaries may search compromised systems to find and obtain insecurely stored credentials. These credentials can be stored and/or misplaced in many locations on a system, including plaintext files (e.g.

name: Credentials In Files
desc: Adversaries may search local file systems and remote file shares for files containing insecurely stored credentials.

name: Credentials in Registry
desc: Adversaries may search the Registry on compromised systems for insecurely stored credentials. The Windows Registry stores configuration information that can be used by the system or other programs.

name: Shell History
desc: Adversaries may search the command history on compromised systems for insecurely stored credentials.

name: Private Keys
desc: Adversaries may search for private key certificate files on compromised systems for insecurely stored credentials. Private cryptographic keys and certificates are used for authentication, encryption/decryption, and digital signatures.

name: Cloud Instance Metadata API
desc: Adversaries may attempt to access the Cloud Instance Metadata API to collect credentials and other sensitive data.

name: Group Policy Preferences
desc: Adversaries may attempt to find unsecured credentials in Group Policy Preferences (GPP). GPP are tools that allow administrators to create domain policies with embedded credentials.

name: Container API
desc: Adversaries may gather credentials via APIs within a containers environment. APIs in these environments, such as the Docker API and Kubernetes APIs, allow a user to remotely manage their container resources and cluster components.

name: Chat Messages
desc: Adversaries may directly collect unsecured credentials stored or passed through user communication services.

name: Subvert Trust Controls
desc: Adversaries may undermine security controls that will either warn users of untrusted activity or prevent execution of untrusted programs.

name: Gatekeeper Bypass
desc: Adversaries may modify file attributes and subvert Gatekeeper functionality to evade user prompts and execute untrusted programs.

name: Code Signing
desc: Adversaries may create, acquire, or steal code signing materials to sign their malware or tools. Code signing provides a level of authenticity on a binary from the developer and a guarantee that the binary has not been tampered with.

name: SIP and Trust Provider Hijacking
desc: Adversaries may tamper with SIP and trust provider components to mislead the operating system and application control tools when conducting signature validation checks.

name: Install Root Certificate
desc: Adversaries may install a root certificate on a compromised system to avoid warnings when connecting to adversary controlled web servers. Root certificates are used in public key cryptography to identify a root certificate authority (CA).

name: Mark-of-the-Web Bypass
desc: Adversaries may abuse specific file formats to subvert Mark-of-the-Web (MOTW) controls.

name: Code Signing Policy Modification
desc: Adversaries may modify code signing policies to enable execution of unsigned or self-signed code. Code signing provides a level of authenticity on a program from a developer and a guarantee that the program has not been tampered with.

name: Compromise Host Software Binary
desc: Adversaries may modify host software binaries to establish persistent access to systems. Software binaries/executables provide a wide range of system commands or services, programs, and libraries.

name: Credentials from Password Stores
desc: Adversaries may search for common password storage locations to obtain user credentials. Passwords are stored in several places on a system, depending on the operating system or application holding the credentials.

name: Keychain
desc: Adversaries may acquire credentials from Keychain. Keychain (or Keychain Services) is the macOS credential management system that stores account names, passwords, private keys, certificates, sensitive application data, payment data, and sec

name: Securityd Memory
desc: An adversary with root access may gather credentials by reading `securityd`’s memory. `securityd` is a service/daemon responsible for implementing security protocols such as encryption and authorization.

name: Credentials from Web Browsers
desc: Adversaries may acquire credentials from web browsers by reading files specific to the target browser.

name: Windows Credential Manager
desc: Adversaries may acquire credentials from the Windows Credential Manager. The Credential Manager stores credentials for signing into websites, applications, and/or devices that request authentication through NTLM or Kerberos in Credential Lo

name: Password Managers
desc: Adversaries may acquire user credentials from third-party password managers. Password managers are applications designed to store user credentials, normally in an encrypted database.

name: Cloud Secrets Management Stores
desc: Adversaries may acquire credentials from cloud-native secret management solutions such as AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault, and Terraform Vault.

name: Modify Authentication Process
desc: Adversaries may modify authentication mechanisms and processes to access user credentials or enable otherwise unwarranted access to accounts.

name: Domain Controller Authentication
desc: Adversaries may patch the authentication process on a domain controller to bypass the typical authentication mechanisms and enable access to accounts.

name: Password Filter DLL
desc: Adversaries may register malicious password filter dynamic link libraries (DLLs) into the authentication process to acquire user credentials as they are validated.

name: Pluggable Authentication Modules
desc: Adversaries may modify pluggable authentication modules (PAM) to access user credentials or enable otherwise unwarranted access to accounts.

name: Network Device Authentication
desc: Adversaries may use Patch System Image to hard code a password in the operating system, thus bypassing of native authentication mechanisms for local accounts on network devices.

name: Reversible Encryption
desc: An adversary may abuse Active Directory authentication encryption properties to gain access to credentials on Windows systems.

name: Multi-Factor Authentication
desc: Adversaries may disable or modify multi-factor authentication (MFA) mechanisms to enable persistent access to compromised accounts.

name: Hybrid Identity
desc: Adversaries may patch, modify, or otherwise backdoor cloud authentication processes that are tied to on-premises user identities in order to bypass typical authentication mechanisms, access credentials, and enable persistent access to accou

name: Network Provider DLL
desc: Adversaries may register malicious network provider dynamic link libraries (DLLs) to capture cleartext user credentials during the authentication process.

name: Conditional Access Policies
desc: Adversaries may disable or modify conditional access policies to enable persistent access to compromised accounts.

name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
desc: Adversaries may attempt to position themselves between two or more networked devices using an adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) technique to support follow-on behaviors such as Network Sniffing, Transmitted Data Manipulation, or replay attacks

name: Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay
desc: By responding to LLMNR/NBT-NS/mDNS network traffic, adversaries may spoof an authoritative source for name resolution to force communication with an adversary controlled system.

name: ARP Cache Poisoning
desc: Adversaries may poison Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) caches to position themselves between the communication of two or more networked devices.

name: DHCP Spoofing
desc: Adversaries may redirect network traffic to adversary-owned systems by spoofing Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) traffic and acting as a malicious DHCP server on the victim network.

name: Evil Twin
desc: Adversaries may host seemingly genuine Wi-Fi access points to deceive users into connecting to malicious networks as a way of supporting follow-on behaviors such as Network Sniffing, Transmitted Data Manipulation, or Input Capture.

name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
desc: Adversaries may attempt to subvert Kerberos authentication by stealing or forging Kerberos tickets to enable Pass the Ticket. Kerberos is an authentication protocol widely used in modern Windows domain environments.

name: Golden Ticket
desc: Adversaries who have the KRBTGT account password hash may forge Kerberos ticket-granting tickets (TGT), also known as a golden ticket.

name: Silver Ticket
desc: Adversaries who have the password hash of a target service account (e.g. SharePoint, MSSQL) may forge Kerberos ticket granting service (TGS) tickets, also known as silver tickets. Kerberos TGS tickets are also known as service tickets.

name: Kerberoasting
desc: Adversaries may abuse a valid Kerberos ticket-granting ticket (TGT) or sniff network traffic to obtain a ticket-granting service (TGS) ticket that may be vulnerable to Brute Force.

name: AS-REP Roasting
desc: Adversaries may reveal credentials of accounts that have disabled Kerberos preauthentication by Password Cracking Kerberos messages. Preauthentication offers protection against offline Password Cracking.

name: Ccache Files
desc: Adversaries may attempt to steal Kerberos tickets stored in credential cache files (or ccache). These files are used for short term storage of a user's active session credentials.

name: Inter-Process Communication
desc: Adversaries may abuse inter-process communication (IPC) mechanisms for local code or command execution. IPC is typically used by processes to share data, communicate with each other, or synchronize execution.

name: Component Object Model
desc: Adversaries may use the Windows Component Object Model (COM) for local code execution.

name: Dynamic Data Exchange
desc: Adversaries may use Windows Dynamic Data Exchange (DDE) to execute arbitrary commands. DDE is a client-server protocol for one-time and/or continuous inter-process communication (IPC) between applications.

name: XPC Services
desc: Adversaries can provide malicious content to an XPC service daemon for local code execution.

name: Archive Collected Data
desc: An adversary may compress and/or encrypt data that is collected prior to exfiltration. Compressing the data can help to obfuscate the collected data and minimize the amount of data sent over the network.

name: Archive via Utility
desc: Adversaries may use utilities to compress and/or encrypt collected data prior to exfiltration. Many utilities include functionalities to compress, encrypt, or otherwise package data into a format that is easier/more secure to transport.

name: Archive via Library
desc: An adversary may compress or encrypt data that is collected prior to exfiltration using 3rd party libraries. Many libraries exist that can archive data, including Python rarfile , libzip , and zlib .

name: Archive via Custom Method
desc: An adversary may compress or encrypt data that is collected prior to exfiltration using a custom method.

name: Disk Wipe
desc: Adversaries may wipe or corrupt raw disk data on specific systems or in large numbers in a network to interrupt availability to system and network resources.

name: Disk Content Wipe
desc: Adversaries may erase the contents of storage devices on specific systems or in large numbers in a network to interrupt availability to system and network resources.

name: Disk Structure Wipe
desc: Adversaries may corrupt or wipe the disk data structures on a hard drive necessary to boot a system; targeting specific critical systems or in large numbers in a network to interrupt availability to system and network resources.

name: Remote Service Session Hijacking
desc: Adversaries may take control of preexisting sessions with remote services to move laterally in an environment.

name: SSH Hijacking
desc: Adversaries may hijack a legitimate user's SSH session to move laterally within an environment. Secure Shell (SSH) is a standard means of remote access on Linux and macOS systems.

name: RDP Hijacking
desc: Adversaries may hijack a legitimate user’s remote desktop session to move laterally within an environment. Remote desktop is a common feature in operating systems.

name: Hide Artifacts
desc: Adversaries may attempt to hide artifacts associated with their behaviors to evade detection.

name: Hidden Files and Directories
desc: Adversaries may set files and directories to be hidden to evade detection mechanisms. To prevent normal users from accidentally changing special files on a system, most operating systems have the concept of a ‘hidden’ file.

name: Hidden Users
desc: Adversaries may use hidden users to hide the presence of user accounts they create or modify.

name: Hidden Window
desc: Adversaries may use hidden windows to conceal malicious activity from the plain sight of users. In some cases, windows that would typically be displayed when an application carries out an operation can be hidden.

name: NTFS File Attributes
desc: Adversaries may use NTFS file attributes to hide their malicious data in order to evade detection.

name: Hidden File System
desc: Adversaries may use a hidden file system to conceal malicious activity from users and security tools. File systems provide a structure to store and access data from physical storage.

name: Run Virtual Instance
desc: Adversaries may carry out malicious operations using a virtual instance to avoid detection. A wide variety of virtualization technologies exist that allow for the emulation of a computer or computing environment.

name: VBA Stomping
desc: Adversaries may hide malicious Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) payloads embedded within MS Office documents by replacing the VBA source code with benign data.

name: Email Hiding Rules
desc: Adversaries may use email rules to hide inbound emails in a compromised user's mailbox.

name: Resource Forking
desc: Adversaries may abuse resource forks to hide malicious code or executables to evade detection and bypass security applications.

name: Process Argument Spoofing
desc: Adversaries may attempt to hide process command-line arguments by overwriting process memory.

name: Ignore Process Interrupts
desc: Adversaries may evade defensive mechanisms by executing commands that hide from process interrupt signals. Many operating systems use signals to deliver messages to control process behavior.

name: File/Path Exclusions
desc: Adversaries may attempt to hide their file-based artifacts by writing them to specific folders or file names excluded from antivirus (AV) scanning and other defensive capabilities.

name: Bind Mounts
desc: Adversaries may abuse bind mounts on file structures to hide their activity and artifacts from native utilities. A bind mount maps a directory or file from one location on the filesystem to another, similar to a shortcut on Windows.

name: Extended Attributes
desc: Adversaries may abuse extended attributes (xattrs) on macOS and Linux to hide their malicious data in order to evade detection. Extended attributes are key-value pairs of file and directory metadata used by both macOS and Linux.

name: Data Manipulation
desc: Adversaries may insert, delete, or manipulate data in order to influence external outcomes or hide activity, thus threatening the integrity of the data.

name: Stored Data Manipulation
desc: Adversaries may insert, delete, or manipulate data at rest in order to influence external outcomes or hide activity, thus threatening the integrity of the data.

name: Transmitted Data Manipulation
desc: Adversaries may alter data en route to storage or other systems in order to manipulate external outcomes or hide activity, thus threatening the integrity of the data.

name: Runtime Data Manipulation
desc: Adversaries may modify systems in order to manipulate the data as it is accessed and displayed to an end user, thus threatening the integrity of the data.

name: Phishing
desc: Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing.

name: Spearphishing Attachment
desc: Adversaries may send spearphishing emails with a malicious attachment in an attempt to gain access to victim systems. Spearphishing attachment is a specific variant of spearphishing.

name: Spearphishing Link
desc: Adversaries may send spearphishing emails with a malicious link in an attempt to gain access to victim systems. Spearphishing with a link is a specific variant of spearphishing.

name: Spearphishing via Service
desc: Adversaries may send spearphishing messages via third-party services in an attempt to gain access to victim systems. Spearphishing via service is a specific variant of spearphishing.

name: Spearphishing Voice
desc: Adversaries may use voice communications to ultimately gain access to victim systems. Spearphishing voice is a specific variant of spearphishing.

name: Exfiltration Over Web Service
desc: Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service to exfiltrate data rather than their primary command and control channel.

name: Exfiltration to Code Repository
desc: Adversaries may exfiltrate data to a code repository rather than over their primary command and control channel. Code repositories are often accessible via an API (ex: https://api.github.com).

name: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage
desc: Adversaries may exfiltrate data to a cloud storage service rather than over their primary command and control channel.

name: Exfiltration to Text Storage Sites
desc: Adversaries may exfiltrate data to text storage sites instead of their primary command and control channel. Text storage sites, such as pastebin[.]com, are commonly used by developers to share code and other information.

name: Exfiltration Over Webhook
desc: Adversaries may exfiltrate data to a webhook endpoint rather than over their primary command and control channel.

name: Dynamic Resolution
desc: Adversaries may dynamically establish connections to command and control infrastructure to evade common detections and remediations.

name: Fast Flux DNS
desc: Adversaries may use Fast Flux DNS to hide a command and control channel behind an array of rapidly changing IP addresses linked to a single domain resolution.

name: Domain Generation Algorithms
desc: Adversaries may make use of Domain Generation Algorithms (DGAs) to dynamically identify a destination domain for command and control traffic rather than relying on a list of static IP addresses or domains.

name: DNS Calculation
desc: Adversaries may perform calculations on addresses returned in DNS results to determine which port and IP address to use for command and control, rather than relying on a predetermined port number or the actual returned IP address.

name: System Services
desc: Adversaries may abuse system services or daemons to execute commands or programs. Adversaries can execute malicious content by interacting with or creating services either locally or remotely.

name: Launchctl
desc: Adversaries may abuse launchctl to execute commands or programs. Launchctl interfaces with launchd, the service management framework for macOS.

name: Service Execution
desc: Adversaries may abuse the Windows service control manager to execute malicious commands or payloads. The Windows service control manager (services.exe) is an interface to manage and manipulate services.

name: Systemctl
desc: Adversaries may abuse systemctl to execute commands or programs. Systemctl is the primary interface for systemd, the Linux init system and service manager.

name: Lateral Tool Transfer
desc: Adversaries may transfer tools or other files between systems in a compromised environment.

name: Non-Standard Port
desc: Adversaries may communicate using a protocol and port pairing that are typically not associated. For example, HTTPS over port 8088 or port 587 as opposed to the traditional port 443.

name: Protocol Tunneling
desc: Adversaries may tunnel network communications to and from a victim system within a separate protocol to avoid detection/network filtering and/or enable access to otherwise unreachable systems.

name: Encrypted Channel
desc: Adversaries may employ an encryption algorithm to conceal command and control traffic rather than relying on any inherent protections provided by a communication protocol.

name: Symmetric Cryptography
desc: Adversaries may employ a known symmetric encryption algorithm to conceal command and control traffic rather than relying on any inherent protections provided by a communication protocol.

name: Asymmetric Cryptography
desc: Adversaries may employ a known asymmetric encryption algorithm to conceal command and control traffic rather than relying on any inherent protections provided by a communication protocol.

name: Hijack Execution Flow
desc: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking the way operating systems run programs. Hijacking execution flow can be for the purposes of persistence, since this hijacked execution may reoccur over time.

name: DLL
desc: Adversaries may abuse dynamic-link library files (DLLs) in order to achieve persistence, escalate privileges, and evade defenses. DLLs are libraries that contain code and data that can be simultaneously utilized by multiple programs.

name: Dylib Hijacking
desc: Adversaries may execute their own payloads by placing a malicious dynamic library (dylib) with an expected name in a path a victim application searches at runtime.

name: Executable Installer File Permissions Weakness
desc: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking the binaries used by an installer. These processes may automatically execute specific binaries as part of their functionality or to perform other actions.

name: Dynamic Linker Hijacking
desc: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking environment variables the dynamic linker uses to load shared libraries.

name: Path Interception by PATH Environment Variable
desc: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking environment variables used to load libraries.

name: Path Interception by Search Order Hijacking
desc: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking the search order used to load other programs.

name: Path Interception by Unquoted Path
desc: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking vulnerable file path references.

name: Services File Permissions Weakness
desc: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking the binaries used by services. Adversaries may use flaws in the permissions of Windows services to replace the binary that is executed upon service start.

name: Services Registry Permissions Weakness
desc: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking the Registry entries used by services.

name: COR_PROFILER
desc: Adversaries may leverage the COR_PROFILER environment variable to hijack the execution flow of programs that load the .NET CLR.

name: KernelCallbackTable
desc: Adversaries may abuse the KernelCallbackTable of a process to hijack its execution flow in order to run their own payloads.

name: AppDomainManager
desc: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking how the .NET `AppDomainManager` loads assemblies.

name: Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure
desc: An adversary may attempt to modify a cloud account's compute service infrastructure to evade defenses.

name: Create Snapshot
desc: An adversary may create a snapshot or data backup within a cloud account to evade defenses. A snapshot is a point-in-time copy of an existing cloud compute component such as a virtual machine (VM), virtual hard drive, or volume.

name: Create Cloud Instance
desc: An adversary may create a new instance or virtual machine (VM) within the compute service of a cloud account to evade defenses.

name: Delete Cloud Instance
desc: An adversary may delete a cloud instance after they have performed malicious activities in an attempt to evade detection and remove evidence of their presence.

name: Revert Cloud Instance
desc: An adversary may revert changes made to a cloud instance after they have performed malicious activities in attempt to evade detection and remove evidence of their presence.

name: Modify Cloud Compute Configurations
desc: Adversaries may modify settings that directly affect the size, locations, and resources available to cloud compute infrastructure in order to evade defenses.

name: Cloud Infrastructure Discovery
desc: An adversary may attempt to discover infrastructure and resources that are available within an infrastructure-as-a-service (IaaS) environment.

name: Acquire Infrastructure
desc: Adversaries may buy, lease, rent, or obtain infrastructure that can be used during targeting. A wide variety of infrastructure exists for hosting and orchestrating adversary operations.

name: Domains
desc: Adversaries may acquire domains that can be used during targeting. Domain names are the human readable names used to represent one or more IP addresses. They can be purchased or, in some cases, acquired for free.

name: DNS Server
desc: Adversaries may set up their own Domain Name System (DNS) servers that can be used during targeting.

name: Virtual Private Server
desc: Adversaries may rent Virtual Private Servers (VPSs) that can be used during targeting. There exist a variety of cloud service providers that will sell virtual machines/containers as a service.

name: Server
desc: Adversaries may buy, lease, rent, or obtain physical servers that can be used during targeting. Use of servers allows an adversary to stage, launch, and execute an operation.

name: Botnet
desc: Adversaries may buy, lease, or rent a network of compromised systems that can be used during targeting. A botnet is a network of compromised systems that can be instructed to perform coordinated tasks.

name: Web Services
desc: Adversaries may register for web services that can be used during targeting. A variety of popular websites exist for adversaries to register for a web-based service that can be abused during later stages of the adversary lifecycle, such as

name: Serverless
desc: Adversaries may purchase and configure serverless cloud infrastructure, such as Cloudflare Workers, AWS Lambda functions, or Google Apps Scripts, that can be used during targeting.

name: Malvertising
desc: Adversaries may purchase online advertisements that can be abused to distribute malware to victims.

name: Compromise Infrastructure
desc: Adversaries may compromise third-party infrastructure that can be used during targeting. Infrastructure solutions include physical or cloud servers, domains, network devices, and third-party web and DNS services.

name: Domains
desc: Adversaries may hijack domains and/or subdomains that can be used during targeting. Domain registration hijacking is the act of changing the registration of a domain name without the permission of the original registrant.

name: DNS Server
desc: Adversaries may compromise third-party DNS servers that can be used during targeting.

name: Virtual Private Server
desc: Adversaries may compromise third-party Virtual Private Servers (VPSs) that can be used during targeting. There exist a variety of cloud service providers that will sell virtual machines/containers as a service.

name: Server
desc: Adversaries may compromise third-party servers that can be used during targeting. Use of servers allows an adversary to stage, launch, and execute an operation.

name: Botnet

name: Scanning IP Blocks

name: Vulnerability Scanning

name: DNS/Passive DNS

name: Threat Intel Vendors

name: Phishing for Information

name: Spearphishing Service

name: Spearphishing Attachment

name: Spearphishing Link

name: Spearphishing Voice

name: Network Address Translation Traversal
desc: Adversaries may bridge network boundaries by modifying a network device’s Network Address Translation (NAT) configuration.

name: Weaken Encryption
desc: Adversaries may compromise a network device’s encryption capability in order to bypass encryption that would otherwise protect data communications.

name: Reduce Key Space
desc: Adversaries may reduce the level of effort required to decrypt data transmitted over the network by reducing the cipher strength of encrypted communications.

name: Disable Crypto Hardware
desc: Adversaries disable a network device’s dedicated hardware encryption, which may enable them to leverage weaknesses in software encryption in order to reduce the effort involved in collecting, manipulating, and exfiltrating transmitted data.

name: Modify System Image
desc: Adversaries may make changes to the operating system of embedded network devices to weaken defenses and provide new capabilities for themselves.

name: Patch System Image

name: Downgrade System Image
desc: Adversaries may install an older version of the operating system of a network device to weaken security.

name: Data from Configuration Repository

name: SNMP (MIB Dump)

name: Network Device Configuration Dump

name: Web Cookies

name: SAML Tokens

name: Upload Tool

name: Install Digital Certificate
desc: Adversaries may install SSL/TLS certificates that can be used during targeting. SSL/TLS certificates are files that can be installed on servers to enable secure communications between systems.

name: Drive-by Target

name: Link Target

name: SEO Poisoning
desc: Adversaries may poison mechanisms that influence search engine optimization (SEO) to further lure staged capabilities towards potential victims.

name: Container Administration Command
desc: Adversaries may abuse a container administration service to execute commands within a container.

name: Deploy Container
desc: Adversaries may deploy a container into an environment to facilitate execution or evade defenses.

name: Escape to Host
desc: Adversaries may break out of a container or virtualized environment to gain access to the underlying host. This can allow an adversary access to other containerized or virtualized resources from the host level or to the host itself.

name: Build Image on Host
desc: Adversaries may build a container image directly on a host to bypass defenses that monitor for the retrieval of malicious images from a public registry.

name: Container and Resource Discovery
desc: Adversaries may attempt to discover containers and other resources that are available within a containers environment. Other resources may include images, deployments, pods, nodes, and other information such as the status of a cluster.

name: System Location Discovery
desc: Adversaries may gather information in an attempt to calculate the geographical location of a victim host.

name: System Language Discovery
desc: Adversaries may attempt to gather information about the system language of a victim in order to infer the geographical location of that host.

name: Cloud Storage Object Discovery
desc: Adversaries may enumerate objects in cloud storage infrastructure. Adversaries may use this information during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors, including requesting all or specific objects from cloud storage.

name: Reflective Code Loading
desc: Adversaries may reflectively load code into a process in order to conceal the execution of malicious payloads.

name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
desc: Adversaries may attempt to bypass multi-factor authentication (MFA) mechanisms and gain access to accounts by generating MFA requests sent to users.

name: Debugger Evasion

name: Plist File Modification

name: Serverless Execution

name: Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates
desc: Adversaries may steal or forge certificates used for authentication to access remote systems or resources. Digital certificates are often used to sign and encrypt messages and/or files.

name: Acquire Access

name: Cloud Administration Command
desc: Adversaries may abuse cloud management services to execute commands within virtual machines.

name: Power Settings

name: Content Injection

name: Hide Infrastructure
desc: Adversaries may manipulate network traffic in order to hide and evade detection of their C2 infrastructure.

name: Modify Cloud Resource Hierarchy
desc: Adversaries may attempt to modify hierarchical structures in infrastructure-as-a-service (IaaS) environments in order to evade defenses.

name: Email Bombing
desc: Adversaries may flood targeted email addresses with an overwhelming volume of messages. This may bury legitimate emails in a flood of spam and disrupt business operations.

name: Cloud Application Integration

desc: Adversaries may manipulate continuous integration / continuous development (CI/CD) processes by injecting malicious code into the build process.

name: Delay Execution
desc: Adversaries may employ various time-based methods to evade detection and analysis. These techniques often exploit system clocks, delays, or timing mechanisms to obscure malicious activity, blend in with benign activity, and avoid scrutiny.

name: Selective Exclusion

name: Local Storage Discovery

name: Disable or Modify Cloud Log
desc: An adversary may disable or modify cloud logging capabilities and integrations to limit what data is collected on their activities and avoid detection.

name: Modify or Spoof Tool UI
desc: Adversaries may spoof or manipulate security tool user interfaces (UIs) to falsely indicate tools are functioning normally and delay detection and response.

name: Windows Host Firewall
desc: Adversaries may disable or modify the Windows host firewall to bypass controls limiting network usage.

desc: Adversaries may exploit vulnerabilities in security software, infrastructure, or defensive components to degrade, disable, or otherwise continue to impair their ability to prevent, detect, or respond to malicious activity.

name: Safe Mode Boot
desc: Adversaries may abuse Windows safe mode to disable endpoint defenses. Safe mode starts up the Windows operating system with a limited set of drivers and services.

name: Downgrade Attack
desc: Adversaries may downgrade or use a version of system features that may be outdated, vulnerable, and/or does not support updated security controls.

name: Prevent Command History Logging
desc: Adversaries may impair command history logging to hide commands they run on a compromised system. Various command interpreters keep track of the commands users type in their terminal so that users can retrace what they have done.
